newsitem.title: USA: Austrian minister sees 10-11 nations in EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Austrian minister sees 10-11 nations in EMU start.

text.p: Austrian Economy Minister Hannes Farnleitner voiced confidence on Wednesday that European monetary union will be launched on time, with 10 or 11 countries participating, including Austria.
"The euro is fixed," he told a small group of reporters here. "(Economic) convergence has happened."

The 15-nation European Union plans to launch a single currency in 1999. Under the Maastricht Treaty, countries that wish to participate from the start must meet budget and other economic criteria this year.
Farnleitner said that Greece will not qualify and that Britain, Sweden and Denmark will likely count themselves out. But all the rest of the EU members could join from the start.

"For us, it's quite sure we'll meet the Maastricht criteria without any problem," the minister said. That includes the requirement that budget deficits be reduced to the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product.
Farnleitner said he expects that criteria will anyway be interpreted to allow countries with deficits slightly above the three percent reference range to join, say, 3.2 percent.
Austria plans to argue that such a flexible interpretation is justified in light of the difficulties in measuring GDP, where initial data often end up being revised later.
Farnleitner said that the new European currency, the euro, has won much more acceptance in international capital markets than it has among the populations of the countries concerned.
He expects Austrian opponents of EMU to garner enough support to force a referendum on monetary union next year, but he added that the vote would be non-binding.

The Austrian minister supported efforts to put more of Europe's focus on fighting unemployment. "Quite a lot of European countries are becoming politically unstable because of high unemployment," he said.
He expects Austrian economic growth to pick up next year to 2-1/4 to 2-1/2 percent, from about 1.5 percent this year. Growth in 1999 will be close to three percent, he added.
